title: Review: Shapes of molecules (VSEPR); Electronegativity, polarity and intermolecular forces
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for OCR A-level (A) Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: BD03#t4 term and clue written for the game; BD03#t3 term and clue written for the game; BD04#t1 term and clue written for the game; BD04#t3 term and clue written for the game. Questions: BD03#N.6, BD04#N.7a, BD03#N.5a, BD04#N.12a, BD03#N.9a, BD04#N.4a, BD03#N.3a, BD04#N.14, BD04#N.9a, BD04#N.2a. The matching task revisits terms from the worlds it reviews, in a new mix. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Octahedral
items.clue: Shape for six pairs, as in SF₆, with every angle 90°.

items.label: Trigonal bipyramidal
items.clue: Shape for five pairs, as in PCl₅, with angles of 120° and 90°.

items.label: Electronegativity
items.clue: The ability of an atom to attract the bonding pair in a covalent bond.

items.label: London forces
items.clue: Electron movement makes a temporary dipole that induces one in a nearby molecule.

questions.stem: Which molecule has four electron pairs arranged tetrahedrally around its central atom, but a non-linear (bent) shape?

options.text: SO₂
CH₄
NH₃
H₂S

questions.explanation: S has two bonding pairs and two lone pairs, like O in water: tetrahedral arrangement, and the atoms H–S–H are bent.

questions.stem: Liquid methanol, CH₃OH, contains hydrogen bonds. What is a hydrogen bond in methanol?

options.text: An attraction between the H of an O–H group and a lone pair on O in another molecule
The covalent bond between the O atom and the H atom within one methanol molecule
An attraction between the H atoms of one molecule and the H atoms of another
An attraction between an H atom of the CH₃ group and an O atom in a neighbouring molecule

questions.explanation: H bonded to O is δ+, and it is attracted to a lone pair on the O of a neighbour.

questions.stem: Predict the H–O–H bond angle in a water molecule, H₂O.

options.text: About 104.5°, as lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs do
About 109.5°, as all four electron pairs around O repel one another equally
About 180°, as the two bonding pairs get as far apart as possible
About 90°, as the H atoms are drawn at right angles in its dot-and-cross diagram

questions.explanation: Two bonding pairs and two lone pairs, arranged tetrahedrally. The lone pairs repel more, squeezing the angle below 109.5°.

questions.stem: Ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH, mixes with water in all proportions, but hexane, C₆H₁₄, does not dissolve in water. Which statement explains this difference?

options.text: Ethanol splits into ions that water surrounds, but hexane does not form ions
Ethanol can form hydrogen bonds with water molecules, but hexane cannot
Hexane is less dense than water, so it floats on the water rather than dissolving
Hexane molecules are too large to fit into the gaps between water molecules

questions.explanation: Ethanol's O–H hydrogen bonds to water, replacing the ones broken. Hexane offers only weak London forces.

questions.stem: In xenon tetrafluoride, XeF₄, the xenon atom (eight outer electrons) forms a single bond to each of four fluorine atoms. What is the shape of XeF₄?

options.text: Tetrahedral, as only its four bonding pairs repel one another around the Xe atom
Octahedral, as there are six electron pairs around the xenon atom
Square planar, as the two lone pairs occupy opposite positions of an octahedron
See-saw, as the two lone pairs occupy adjacent positions, 90° apart, in an octahedron

questions.explanation: 8 − 4 = 4 non-bonding electrons: two lone pairs. They sit 180° apart, leaving four F in a square plane.

questions.stem: Water, H₂O, is a polar molecule with a permanent dipole (electronegativity: H 2.2, O 3.4). Which statement explains this?

options.text: Its O–H bonds are polar, and every molecule with polar bonds has a permanent dipole
It is bent, so its two O–H bond dipoles do not point in opposite directions
Its H atoms lie at 90° to each other, as in its dot-and-cross diagram, so the dipoles add
Its oxygen atom has two lone pairs, which are the only source of its permanent dipole

questions.explanation: Each O–H is δ− at O. At about 104.5° the two dipoles add to a resultant.

questions.stem: Ammonia, NH₃, has three bonding pairs and one lone pair around the nitrogen atom. What is its shape?

options.text: Tetrahedral, as there are four electron pairs around the nitrogen atom
Trigonal planar, as only the three bonding pairs repel one another
Flat, with 90° bond angles, as the atoms are drawn in its dot-and-cross diagram on paper
Pyramidal (trigonal pyramidal), as the lone pair occupies one of four tetrahedral positions

questions.explanation: Four pairs point to the corners of a tetrahedron. Atoms sit at three of them, so N is at the top of a pyramid: about 107°.

questions.stem: Ammonia, NH₃ (Mᵣ 17.0), boils at −33 °C. Phosphine, PH₃ (Mᵣ 34.0), boils at −88 °C. Electronegativity: H 2.2, N 3.0, P 2.2. Why does the lighter molecule boil higher?

options.text: PH₃ molecules have no forces between them, because their P–H bonds are non-polar.
NH₃ has stronger London forces than PH₃, because it is the smaller molecule.
NH₃ molecules hydrogen bond to each other; PH₃ molecules cannot.
Boiling NH₃ breaks its N–H bonds, which are stronger than P–H bonds.

questions.explanation: N is very electronegative, so N–H is δ+ at H, and each N has a lone pair: N–H⋯N hydrogen bonds. P–H bonds are hardly polar (both 2.2), so PH₃ has no hydrogen bonds.

questions.stem: Propane, CH₃CH₂CH₃ (Mᵣ 44.11), ethanal, CH₃CHO (Mᵣ 44.06), and ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH (Mᵣ 46.08), have comparable molar masses. Which lists them in order of increasing boiling point?

options.text: propane < ethanal < ethanol
propane < ethanol < ethanal
ethanal < propane < ethanol
ethanal < ethanol < propane

questions.explanation: Similar masses, so the force type decides: London only (−42 °C), dipole–dipole added (20 °C), hydrogen bonds (78 °C).

questions.stem: Electronegativity values: H 2.2, C 2.6, O 3.4, F 4.0, P 2.2. Which bond is the most polar?

options.text: O–H
O–F
C–F
P–H

questions.explanation: 4.0 − 2.6 = 1.4, the largest difference, so the pair is pulled most towards F.
